Abstract 16

Magneto-elastic Granular Architectures (MEGAs) consisting of 3D-printed star- 17 shaped units and magnetic branch termini oﬀer modularity and reversibility 18 not seen in conventional monolithic materials. Tailoring magnetic strength and 19 star topology leads to ordered structures with distinct mechanical responses. 20 However, single-component MEGAs typically exhibit limited tensile extensibil- 21 ity. Here we show that binary superlattices, introduced by combining two-branch 22 (Bar) and three-branch (Y) units, enable programmable tensile strength and 23 ductility and yield architectures with extensibility far exceeding that of single- 24 component systems. By tuning unit sizes, we uncover hierarchical dual networks 25 in which subnetwork units provide hidden length released via sacriﬁcial mag- 26 netic bond detachment during deformation. We construct a phase diagram, a 27 performance map, and a predictive framework to reveal design rules linking unit 28 geometry, deformation pathways, and macroscopic response. Our work opens 29 opportunities for easy-to-assemble and reconﬁgurable architected metamateri- 30 als with controllable brittle–ductile transitions, with implications for adaptive 31 load-bearing, impact mitigation, and robotic systems. 32

1 Introduction 35

Soft magneto-elastic materials exhibit intriguing mechanical properties arising from 36 the coupling between magnetic and elastic interactions during deformation. Exter- 37 nal stimuli such as stress or magnetic ﬁelds can induce large conﬁgurational changes, 38 enabling multifunctional [1, 2], reconﬁgurable [3, 4], and mechanically adaptive 39 responses [5, 6]. These capabilities unlock a broad range of applications, from wearable 40 devices for energy harvesting and motion sensing [7, 8] to architected metamaterials 41 exhibiting auxeticity [9–11], impact resistance [12, 13], and programmable shape- 42 morphing [14, 15]. Despite their promise across diverse ﬁelds, from soft robotics to 43 non-invasive surgery, most magneto-elastic designs rely on embedding magnetic inclu- 44 sions within a continuous monolithic soft matrix [9, 10, 15–18], which limits modularity 45 and reversibility. By contrast, granular or unit-based designs as commonly utilized in 46 magnetic builder toys oﬀer tremendous advantages over monolithic designs because 47 they are reusable and reconﬁgurable for diﬀerent purposes. However, they typically suf- 48 fer from low tensile strength and ductility, restricting their applicability in mechanical 49 systems. 50 To address the inherent limitations of monolithic magneto-elastic materials, we pre- 51 viously introduced a unit-based self-assembly approach to construct two-dimensional 52 (2D) magneto-elastic granular architectures (MEGAs) [19–21]. These systems consist 53 of star-shaped units with magnetic branch termini, whose reversible magnetic inter- 54 actions enable repeated assembly–disassembly cycles without damage to individual 55 units. As a result, MEGAs exhibit on-the-ﬂy reconﬁgurability and healability, capable 56 of recovering their original conﬁguration and functionality upon shaking [19, 20], or so- 57 called thermalization in the context of granular mechanics. Single-component MEGAs 58 form diverse ordered lattices with high strength and stiﬀness [19, 20, 22], but a key 59 shortcoming is that magnetic bonds along weak planes tend to detach simultaneously 60 and catastrophically under tensile loading, signiﬁcantly reducing their deformation 61 capacity and overall toughness [20]. 62 More broadly, overcoming the strength–toughness trade-oﬀremains a central chal- 63 lenge across architected metamaterials, as highlighted in recent work [23–25]. In a wide 64 range of material systems, introducing compositional or structural heterogeneity has 65 proven eﬀective in mitigating this trade-oﬀ, as demonstrated in high-entropy alloys 66 with multiple principal elements [26–28], multi-component polymeric composites [29– 67

31], and hierarchical biomimetic materials [32–34]. These studies suggest that such 68 heterogeneity can fundamentally alter deformation pathways and failure mechanisms. 69 However, whether these concepts can be translated to granular architected systems, 70 particularly without altering the fundamental unit design, remains largely unexplored. 71

Here, we show that binary superlattices signiﬁcantly enhance the limited tensile 72 extensibility of single-component MEGAs and enable programmable strength and duc- 73 tility. Building on prior MEGA designs [19–21], we combine two-branch (Bar) and 74 three-branch (Y) units and tune their relative sizes to form hierarchical dual networks. 75 In these systems, subnetwork units provide hidden length released via sacriﬁcial mag- 76 netic bond detachment during deformation, resulting in exceptional tensile ductility 77 not typically seen in granular materials. To systematically characterize this behavior 78 and its programmability, we construct a phase diagram, a performance map, and a 79 predictive framework, supported by simulations, experiments, and machine learning, 80 to identify design rules linking unit geometry, deformation pathways, and macroscopic 81 response. Our results establish a general strategy for designing easy-to-assemble and 82 reconﬁgurable architected metamaterials with controllable brittle–ductile transitions, 83 providing a pathway to adaptive structures and modular soft robotic assemblies that 84 dynamically balance strength and toughness. 85

2 Results 86

2.1 Equilibrated binary MEGA superlattices 87

The general features of a 2D MEGA unit are illustrated in Fig. 1a. Each unit consists 88 of a star-shaped elastic framework with n branches of length L0 and equal angular 89 separation α (α = 2π/n), whose tips carry diametrically magnetized cylinder magnets 90 modeled as point dipoles with prescribed orientation ϕ [35]. Three-dimensional (3D) 91 realizations of MEGA units with 2 (Bar) and 3 (Y) branches are shown in Fig. 1b, 92 where magnets are ﬁxed in tapered mounting holes. Prior studies established that 93 MEGA units with varying star topologies self-assemble into diverse lattice structures 94 with distinct mechanical responses, including auxeticity and crack redirection [19, 20, 95

22]. 96 Based on the ﬁnding that single-component Bar and Y systems can form triangu- 97 lar and rhombic lattices, respectively, under appropriate dipole orientations [19, 20], 98 we superpose these conﬁgurations to generate binary Bar–Y systems and perform 99 free equilibration (annealing) simulations. The unit conﬁgurations of the Bar and Y 100 units used in this study are shown in Fig. 1c, with dipoles at branch termini indi- 101 cated by red arrows. During equilibration, the superposed systems either contract into 102 dense lattices or expand into low-density networks. The phase map in Fig. 1d sum- 103 marizes the resulting states across the selected ranges of Bar branch length L0,Bar 104 and Y branch length L0,Y, revealing three contracted regimes (regions I–III) and one 105 expanded regime (region E) that appears in two disconnected zones. 106 In region I (blue), Bar units organize into a primary triangular lattice, with nodes 107 formed by six Bar ends binding together and smaller Y units occupying interstitial 108 voids (e.g., systems I-1 to I-3 in Fig. 1e), deﬁning a Bar-dominant regime. The binary 109 lattice pattern is governed by the relative size of the two units. However, their distinct 110 geometries make direct comparison nontrivial. To quantify this, we deﬁne a normalized 111 unit-size diﬀerence, 112

Notably, regions I and III exhibit counterclockwise rotational motifs, whereas region 127 II shows the opposite (clockwise) orientation. 128 Region E contains two transitional zones (gray) between regions I–II and II–III. 129 Here, steric constraints and unfavorable dipole–dipole interactions, which generate 130 strong repulsive forces, prevent the formation of dense contracted conﬁgurations. 131 Instead, these systems relax into low-density expanded hexagonal lattices, with nodes 132 formed by Bars extending linearly from Y branches (e.g., systems E-1 and E-2 in 133 Fig. 1f). These lattices are highly extensible owing to their low bending stiﬀness 134 but mechanically weak due to their low magnetic interaction energy density (Supple- 135 mentary Note 2; Supplementary Video 1). Therefore, subsequent analysis focuses on 136 contracted regimes I–III. 137 Overall, the system evolves from Bar-dominant (region I) to Y-dominant (region 138 III) conﬁgurations as the relative unit size changes, passing through expanded (region 139 E) and balanced (region II) regimes (Fig. 1d). The phase map is thus partitioned 140 into ﬁve bands separated by nearly linear boundaries. Rather than reﬁning these 141 boundaries via extensive simulations on a ﬁner grid of the design space, we employ a 142 machine learning model to capture them eﬃciently, as discussed later. Binary Bar–Y 143 superlattices, composed of 2- and 3-branch units, represent a minimal realization of 144 multi-component MEGAs and provide a foundation for more complex MEGA architec- 145 tures. The results are scalable under uniform geometric rescaling with corresponding 146 adjustments to magnetic strength (Supplementary Note 3). 147

2.2 Mechanical response under uniaxial tension 148

In Fig. 2, we present uniaxial tensile stress–strain responses of three representative 149 binary Bar–Y superlattices selected from the contracted regimes of the phase map. 150 Panel a shows a typical conﬁguration from the balanced-network region (II), whereas 151 panels b and c represent systems from the Bar-dominant (I) and Y-dominant (III) 152 regions with superior tensile ductility. Insets show the undeformed magnetic clus- 153 ters, and characteristic deformed conﬁgurations are shown below the curves. Full 154 deformation trajectories are provided in Supplementary Videos 2–4. 155 We ﬁrst consider Fig. 2a, with (L0,Bar, L0,Y) = (1.9, 2.3). Under uniaxial tension, 156 this system fails in a highly brittle manner. From stage (i) to (ii), cracks initiate and 157 rapidly propagate across the entire lattice, leading to an abrupt loss of load-bearing 158 capacity. This nearly simultaneous detachment of magnetic ends signiﬁcantly limits 159 the tensile ductility in the balanced-network region (II). 160 In contrast, binary systems in Fig. 2b,c adopt hierarchical architectures, where 161 units of one type are embedded within a primary network formed by the other. 162 These embedded units preserve network connectivity after crack initiation and enhance 163 ductility. 164 In Fig. 2b, with (L0,Bar, L0,Y) = (1.4, 1.0), smaller Y units are caged within a 165 triangular lattice formed by larger Bars. During early deformation, fracture of the 166 triangular lattice produces a pronounced stress peak. The Y units then unravel and 167 bridge the diagonal cracks in the primary lattice, maintaining load-bearing capacity. 168 Subsequent random disassembly of Bar and Y units enables continued deformation 169 and increases extensibility. 170

In Fig. 2c, with (L0,Bar, L0,Y) = (1.0, 1.9), Bar units are embedded within a rhom- 171 bic network formed by Y units. Nevertheless, these systems remain mechanically weak due to 200 the twelve-magnet binding motif. 201 Taken together, these results establish a fundamental design strategy for achieving 202 strong and tough MEGA superlattices: inserting secondary units into a primary stiﬀ 203 and brittle network to enhance ductility while preserving strength. 204

2.3 Experimental validation of binary system mechanics 205

Experiments were performed to verify the deformation modes and tensile responses 206 predicted by the simulations. Binary lattices comprising fewer units were fabricated 207 for qualitative comparison, with quantitative mechanical characterization of full-size 208 lattices left for future work. Systems with (L0,Bar, L0,Y) = (1.9, 2.3), (1.4, 1.0), and 209 (1.0, 1.9) were examined, corresponding to those in Fig. 2a–c. The deformations and 210 tensile responses are shown in Fig. 3. For qualitative comparison, force–displacement 211 curves from the experiments are presented directly without conversion to stress–strain 212 relations. 213 The balanced network in Fig. 3a exhibits brittle failure, with a crack initiating 214 at the top and rapidly propagating to the bottom with minimal elongation. The 215 force–displacement curve shows a dominant initial peak followed by a much smaller 216 secondary peak, with a total elongation of only 12 mm, matching the pattern of the 217 simulated response (Fig. 2a). 218 In contrast, both the Bar-dominant and Y-dominant lattices (Fig. 3b,c) show 219 enhanced ductility, where the release of hidden length enables crack bridging and stress 220 redistribution, thereby suppressing rapid crack propagation. 221 The Bar-dominant network in Fig. 3b deforms through localized and repeated mag- 222 net detachment and reattachment. 2.5 Predictive modeling of binary superlattice conﬁgurations 271 and tensile response 272

To generalize these results and demonstrate the programmability of tensile strength 273 and ductility, we present a data-driven framework that predicts assembly conﬁgura- 274 tions and tensile properties of binary MEGA superlattices from unit sizes (Fig. 5a). 275 Taking the branch lengths (L0,Bar, L0,Y) as inputs, a Gaussian process classiﬁer (GPC) 276 ﬁrst determines the system type by identifying the region it falls into, selecting among 277 three contracted regions (Bar-dominant, balanced, and Y-dominant) and one expanded 278 region (Supplementary Fig. 3). Expanded systems, which form low-density hexago- 279 nal lattices with low strength, are excluded from subsequent analysis. In this forward 280 design workﬂow, the GPC acts as a ﬁlter that restricts the design space to strong 281 MEGA superlattices. 282 For contracted systems, the ﬁrst regressor predicts the lattice conﬁguration using a 283 minimal set of geometric parameters, including the x-coordinate of a reference Bar unit 284 (XBar), the center coordinates of the Y unit above it (XY, YY), and their orientation 285 angles (θBar, θY). These parameters deﬁne a magnetic cluster conﬁguration and enable 286 reconstruction of the full binary superlattice (Supplementary Note 5.1). To account for 287 parameter dependencies and region-speciﬁc diﬀerences, we use separate multi-output 288 GPs for each region to learn the mapping from (L0,Bar, L0,Y) to these parameters, 289 achieving high prediction accuracy (Supplementary Note 5.2). 290 Fig. 5b–d compare the predicted and ground-truth magnetic cluster conﬁgurations 291 for three testing samples in the Bar-dominant (b), balanced (c), and Y-dominant 292 (d) regions. Gray and blue dashed outlines represent the ground-truth (simulated) 293 positions and orientations of the Bar and Y units, respectively, while solid shapes 294 show predictions. The close agreement indicates that the model accurately predicts 295 cluster conﬁgurations from unit sizes, providing assembly-ready designs for MEGA 296 superlattices. Because the excluded volume of MEGA units is not explicitly encoded 297 as a constraint, unit collisions may occur (e.g., Fig. 5b), which can be problematic 298 for precise robotic assembly. Therefore, the predicted conﬁgurations are checked for 299 unit overlap. If overlap is detected, a short energy minimization is applied to relax 300 the structure into a physically feasible conﬁguration before using it as the assembly 301 reference. 302 The second regressor predicts tensile strength σu and toughness UT . Considering 303 the highly nonlinear geometry–property relationship (Fig. 4a,b), we employ a neural 304 network to learn this complex mapping (Supplementary Note 5.3). The trained model 305 achieves strong predictive performance on the testing set, with R2 = 0.97 for strength 306 and R2 = 0.70 for toughness (Fig. 5e). The lower accuracy for toughness reﬂects its 307 intrinsically greater variability than strength due to the stochastic nature of fracture 308 behavior [37], which introduces higher noise in the data. 309 The predicted tensile response across the design space suggest that the surrogate 310 model successfully captures the underlying geometry–property relationship (Supple- 311 mentary Note 5.4). By bypassing computationally expensive simulations, the model 312 enables rapid design space exploration for material selection and structural screening. 313 The orange curve in Fig. 5f shows the neural-network predicted Pareto-optimal front 314 between strength and toughness, together with existing samples in the dataset (mean 315

3 Conclusions 326

Building on single-component MEGAs, we use a superposition-based method to 327 construct binary Bar–Y superlattices and systematically explore how lattice conﬁg- 328 urations and tensile responses evolve with the unit sizes. When the two units are 329 comparable in size, balanced networks form and fail in a relatively brittle manner. 330 As the sizes diverge, the binary system transitions into conﬁgurations dominated by 331 the larger units, with the smaller units acting as sublattices within the larger-unit 332 framework. At optimal size combinations, where the diﬀerence in characteristic spans 333 between the two units is approximately ﬁve times the eﬀective radius, the architectures 334 achieve both high strength and toughness. Here, the smaller units progressively unravel 335 to release hidden length, while the larger-unit framework breaks through sacriﬁcial 336 magnetic bonds, leading to a signiﬁcant enhancement in tensile ductility. 337 At these optimal size combinations, a distinct deformation mode emerges when Y 338 units are larger, characterized by a highly extensible multi-peak tensile response arising 339 from the coordinated layer-by-layer unraveling of Bar units. This behavior is absent 340 in the opposite conﬁguration with larger Bars and smaller Ys, where the three-branch 341 Y units, owing to their multiple binding sites, detach and reattach to nearby units 342 stochastically, preventing the formation of ordered deformation pathways. As one unit 343 becomes suﬃciently larger, the response converges to that of the corresponding single- 344 component lattices formed by the larger units. Experimental tensile tests on reduced- 345 size assemblies validate these ﬁndings. A performance map of strength and toughness 346 further oﬀers guidance for designing strong and tough binary MEGA superlattices. 347 To enable predictive design, we develop a data-driven framework that links unit 348 sizes to both MEGA superlattice conﬁgurations and tensile responses, allowing identi- 349 ﬁcation of the Pareto frontier for the strength–toughness trade-oﬀ. While the present 350 study focuses on forward prediction and simple binary systems, future extensions may 351 incorporate additional MEGA unit types, more diverse hierarchical architectures, and 352 sensitivity to magnet strength within the current data-driven framework to enable 353 automated design and assembly. The ultimate goal is to establish a generalized pre- 354 dictive design tool for multi-component MEGA superlattices with tailored mechanical 355 properties across diverse engineering applications. 356 In summary, our ﬁndings demonstrate that organizing MEGAs into binary super- 357 lattices can fundamentally alter deformation modes and push their mechanical limits. 358 We highlight the toughening mechanism that arises from leveraging sacriﬁcial bonds 359 and hidden length within hybrid MEGA superlattices. Our work opens the vast and 360 previously unexplored design space of resilient and reconﬁgurable magneto-elastic 361 architected granular metamaterials. The unit-size-dependent design rules and the 362 predictive modeling framework establish a foundation for the rational design of multi- 363 component MEGAs with programmable conﬁgurations and mechanical properties, 364 making them suitable for diverse applications such as soft robotics, impact mitigation, 365 and protective equipment. 366

4 Methods 367

4.1 Construction of binary MEGA lattices in the simulation 368

The binary Bar–Y systems were generated following the procedure illustrated in Sup- 369 plementary Fig. 4. To achieve an experimentally producible and measurable MEGA 370 assembly, the branch lengths of the Bar unit (L0,Bar) and the Y unit (L0,Y) are set 371 to 1.0–2.0 cm and 1.0–2.5 cm, respectively, with an increment of 0.1 cm. Branches 372 were modeled as non-extensible rigid elements to highlight reversible magnetic interac- 373 tions and improve computational eﬃciency, consistent with the negligible deformation 374 observed in tensile experiments. Fully coupled magneto-elastic eﬀects with extensible 375 branches of variable stiﬀness are left for future exploration. Magnetic dipole moments 376 were calculated based on the properties of the N42 neodymium magnets used in exper- 377 iments (radius 0.15875 cm, height 0.635 cm, mass 0.377 g). To match experimental 378 geometry, the branch tip radius was set to the sum of the magnet radius (0.15875 cm) 379 and a mounting oﬀset (0.08 cm) in the simulation. Initial unit cells were generated 380 by superposing triangular and rhombic lattices corresponding to the ground states of 381 Bar-only and Y-only systems [20]. Unit positions (i.e., unit center coordinates) were 382 uniformly scaled to remove geometric overlaps. To account for orientation bias, three 383 unit-cell variants (clockwise, counterclockwise, and symmetric) were constructed. Each 384 unit cell was then replicated 11 times along x and 6 times along y to form a larger 385 lattice under periodic boundary conditions. 386 Free equilibration was then performed via particle dynamics simulations using the 387 HOOMD-blue (v4.3.0) molecular dynamics package, with branches modeled as rigid 388 bodies [38–40]. Details of the simulation setup follow our previous work [20]. We used 389 a timestep of dt = 2 × 10−7 s and an isothermal–isobaric (NPT) ensemble with zero 390 target stress, a barostat coupling constant of 106dt, and a Nos´e–Hoover thermostat 391 with coupling constant 100dt. Over a total of 1.6 s of simulation time, the thermal 392 noise level, which represents the random noise from the environment, was gradually 393 reduced from 5 × 10−6 J to 10−8 J in four steps, mimicking an annealing process that 394 accelerates relaxation toward favorable local minima of the energy landscape. The cut- 395 oﬀdistance for the magnetic dipole–dipole interaction was set to 7 cm, at which the 396 interaction energy and corresponding force become negligible. For each Bar–Y com- 397 bination, multiple simulations were performed to account for stochastic eﬀects. The 398 equilibrated structures were classiﬁed as either contracted or expanded based on their 399 deformation during equilibration. Near phase boundaries, both conﬁgurations may 400 arise. Such systems were labeled as contracted if any contracted state was observed. 401 Consequently, the resolution of phase boundaries remains limited, as these boundary 402 systems occupy a regime where both conﬁgurations are energetically competitive and 403 highly sensitive to random disturbances. 404

4.2 Quasi-static uniaxial tension simulation 405

The equilibrated binary lattices from the previous steps were subjected to an addi- 406 tional round of free equilibration with periodic boundaries along the x-direction and 407 open boundaries in the transverse direction. Following a procedure similar to the 408

13


<!-- Page 15 -->


quasi-static uniaxial compression simulations demonstrated in our previous study [20], 409 quasi-static uniaxial tensile tests were conducted in the canonical ensemble (NVT) 410 by deforming the simulation box along the x-direction at a constant strain rate of 411 0.02 s−1, which is suﬃciently small to show minimal rate sensitivity. A Nos´e–Hoover 412 thermostat with a trivial thermal noise level of 10−8 J was applied. The tensile stress 413 was measured in the pulling direction throughout the deformation. Each simulation 414 was terminated once a dominant crack fully propagated across the lattice, causing 415 the structure to fragment and lose its entire load-bearing capacity. Stress data were 416 recorded every 0.002 s and smoothed using a moving average with a window size of 10. 417

4.3 Fabrication of MEGA units 418

The fabrication of the Bar and Y units followed a workﬂow adapted from our previous 419 studies [19, 20]. Each unit consists of a 3D-printed holder in Bar or Y shape, and 420 Neodymium cylindrical magnets (D24DIA, K&J Magnetics) press-ﬁtted at each end of 421 the holder’s branches with their dipole orientations ﬁxed according to the design. The 422 branch dimensions were chosen to match those used in the simulations. All holders were 423 printed using a FDM 3D printer (X1C, Bambu Lab) with PLA ﬁlament (PLA Basic, 424 Bambu Lab), a commonly used 3D-printing material with a high tensile modulus of 425 2.58 GPa and low mass density of 1.24 g/cm3. 426

4.4 Quasi-static uniaxial tension experiment 427

A customized testing platform was constructed to perform the uniaxial tensile exper- 428 iment. The setup comprised a ﬁxed gripper connected to a high-sensitivity load cell 429 (FRC4160-0, C2 accuracy grade, Phidget), a moving gripper driven by a linear stage 430 to deform the lattice, and a nonmagnetic aluminum base rail supporting the entire 431 assembly, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 5a,b. In each experiment, a 4 × 1 array 432 of unit cells, corresponding to a subset of the full lattice in the simulation, was used 433 for tensile characterization. Paramagnetic metal plates and screws (Supplementary 434 Fig. 5c) fastened the boundary unit cells to the grippers through their central mag- 435 net rings, enabling the boundary units to move with the moving gripper along the 436 base rail. The two grippers imposed displacement boundary constraints by suppress- 437 ing translation in all non-loading directions while allowing free rotation at both ends, 438 thereby matching the boundary conditions used in the simulations. The displacement 439 applied by the moving gripper was obtained from the linear-stage motion, and the 440 corresponding reaction force was recorded by the load cell. At the beginning of each 441 test, the binary MEGA lattice was positioned between the grippers without preload. 442 It was then pulled quasi-statically at a rate of 2.5 mm/s until complete fragmentation 443 or until the displacement limit of the device was reached. 444

4.5 Machine learning model 445

In the data-driven prediction framework described in the Results, a GPC was ﬁrst 446 employed to determine the conﬁguration type using the branch-length features x = 447 [L0,Bar, L0,Y]. A GPC was chosen for this task because it can provide smooth decision 448 boundaries and probabilistic predictions, enabling reliable classiﬁcation in the presence 449

The kernel is deﬁned 451 as a radial basis function (RBF) kernel multiplied by a constant kernel. The resulting 452 covariance function between two inputs x and x′ takes the form 453

where σ2 f is the amplitude and ℓis the characteristic length scale of the RBF kernel. All 454 kernel hyperparameters were optimized via marginal-likelihood maximization during 455 training. The dataset used in this task contains 176 samples: 51 Bar-dominant, 35 456 balanced, 32 Y-dominant, and 58 expanded conﬁgurations. The data were randomly 457 split into an 80/20 training/testing ratio, and the trained classiﬁer achieved a testing 458 accuracy of 94.4%. Five-fold cross-validation further conﬁrmed the robustness of the 459 model, yielding an average accuracy of 95.5%. 460 Following classiﬁcation, three multi-output GPs were constructed to predict the 461 magnetic cluster conﬁgurations for the Bar-dominant, balanced, and Y-dominant 462 regions, respectively. In this task, x = [L0,Bar, L0,Y] were used as inputs and the ﬁve 463 geometric parameters y = [XBar, XY, YY, θBar, θY] representing the magnetic cluster 464 conﬁguration were used as outputs. Because the multi-output GP jointly models all 465 ﬁve outputs within a shared covariance structure, it explicitly leverages their statisti- 466 cal correlations and is able to capture the inherent relationships among the geometric 467 parameters. The multi-output GPs were implemented in Python using GPyTorch [42]. 468 Each regressor employs a constant mean function and a multi-task kernel consisting 469 of an RBF kernel wrapped in a scale kernel, combined with a rank-1 coregionalization 470 matrix. The likelihood is a multitask Gaussian likelihood with negligible observation 471 noise, consistent with the deterministic nature of the geometric parameters in the 472 dataset. The dataset sizes for the three models are 51 (Bar-dominant), 35 (balanced), 473 and 32 (Y-dominant), respectively. For each model, the data were randomly divided 474 into training and testing subsets using an 80/20 split. The predictive accuracy of the 475 three multi-output GP models is reported in Supplementary Note 5.2. 476 For mechanical property prediction, a neural network was employed to learn the 477 mapping from the geometric features x = [L0,Bar, L0,Y] to the mechanical responses 478 f = [σu, UT ]. The model was implemented in Python using PyTorch. The dataset for 479 this task contains 118 samples, which were randomly divided into 70 training samples, 480 24 validation samples, and 24 testing samples. The network architecture and hyperpa- 481 rameters (activation function) were selected through a grid-search procedure (details 482 provided in Supplementary Note 5.3). The resulting optimal model has a hidden-layer 483 structure of [16,32,16], uses a Sigmoid activation function, and was trained with a 484 learning rate of 5 × 10−4. The network parameters were optimized using the Adam 485 optimizer by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) between predicted and ground- 486 truth properties. The Pareto-front optimization based on the neural network and the 487 Gaussian process classiﬁer (GPC) was performed using the NSGA-II algorithm with 488 a population size of 100. 489
